column11: I am unsure, though, what the incentives of firms are to reward long hours (it is at least not clear in all cases).

Just like some professions disproportionately reward working long and inflexible hours, the same is true of firms working across time zones. The gender wage gap in such firms goes up as the business hour overlap with their export markets goes down.

column8: Agree with the statement for developed and fairly advanced economies.
The "where" issue seems key here. In the US, I'd say almost surely. Portugal? Brazil? Saudi Arabia? Seems far less likely.
column11: It the US at least, increasingly women score better is all sorts of tests than men. A feature of the labor market recently has been a complementarity between talent and hours, effort etc. So its not clear is cutting off that channel harms women, despite their greater family role.
However, the key issue is the origin of firms' incentives to offer disproportionate rewards to individuals who work long and/or inflexible hours?

Reducing firms' possibilities to offer long-hours incentives could backfire by inducing firms to use other means to attract individuals who will work long hours. Firms could for example start doing more (statistical) discrimination at the hiring stage
